q: A team introduced SAST and immediately made it blocking. Within a week developers had added allow_failure: true in most repos. What should have been done differently?
options: Run the tool in informational mode first, measure false positives, then block only new high-severity findings with an agreed exception process
Move SAST to a nightly pipeline so it doesn't bother developers
Forbid allow_failure in all .gitlab-ci.yml files using CODEOWNERS
Replace SAST with DAST because DAST has no false positives
explain: A gradual rollout (informational → blocking for new severe findings) with an exception process preserves developer trust. A nightly pipeline delays feedback, forbidding allow_failure doesn't fix the noise, and DAST doesn't replace SAST and also has false positives.

q: An auditor asks for evidence that the organization follows the NIST SSDF practice for verifying release integrity. Which pipeline artifact is the most direct evidence?
options: The Semgrep SARIF report from the MR pipeline
The job log with unit test results
A cosign signature of the image and signature verification before deploy
The list of open findings in DefectDojo
explain: Verifying release integrity (the PS group, Protect the Software) is proven by an artifact signature and its verification. The Semgrep SARIF is evidence for code analysis (PW), unit tests are not a security control, and the findings list is evidence for RV.

q: Match the pipeline activity with the NIST SSDF practice group it fits best.
options: Protected branches and mandatory review for .gitlab-ci.yml
Semgrep and osv-scanner in every MR
Triage of a new CVE and root cause analysis so the class of bug does not recur
Defining the criterion "a CRITICAL vulnerability blocks the release" and training teams
explain: Protecting code from unauthorized changes is PS, analyzing code and components is PW, responding to vulnerabilities and root cause analysis are RV, and defining criteria, roles and training is PO.

q: The CISO wants an annual assessment of the whole software security program, including governance, education and incident management, with a target profile for next year. Which framework fits best?
options: OWASP DSOMM
OWASP SAMM v2
OWASP Top 10 CI/CD Security Risks
NIST SP 800-218A
explain: SAMM v2 covers 5 business functions (including Governance and Operations) with 15 practices and 3 maturity levels, and is meant for program assessment. DSOMM focuses on technical DevSecOps activities, Top 10 CI/CD is a list of risks, and 800-218A is the SSDF profile for generative AI.

q: A platform team wants a concrete plan of "which security activities we introduce in the pipeline next," grouped by areas such as Build and Deployment and Test and Verification. Which model should they use?
options: NIST SSDF
OWASP SAMM v2
STRIDE
OWASP DSOMM
explain: DSOMM has the dimensions Build and Deployment, Culture and Organization, Implementation, Information Gathering and Test and Verification, with concrete activities per level. SSDF is a practice framework without levels, SAMM is an organizational model, and STRIDE is a threat classification.

q: A colleague claims: "We have shift-left: SAST, SCA and image scanning in the MR. We don't need anything after deploy." Which scenario shows they are wrong?
options: A developer commits a secret the pre-commit hook doesn't recognize
SAST reports a false positive in test code
A month after the release, a CVE is published for a library in an image already running in production
A merge request has too many findings so the reviewer rejects it
explain: A new CVE affects artifacts that have already passed every gate, so you need continuous scanning of the registry and production (shift-right). The other options are problems within shift-left controls, not an argument for controls after deploy.

q: Which statement about NIST SSDF is correct as of October 2026?
options: SSDF prescribes concrete tools, e.g. Semgrep for PW.7
The current final version is SP 800-218 (SSDF 1.1), and SP 800-218 Rev. 1 (SSDF 1.2) was published as a draft in December 2025
SSDF has five practice groups, the same as the SAMM business functions
SSDF has been replaced by OWASP DSOMM
explain: SP 800-218 v1.1 (February 2022) is the final version, and Rev. 1 (SSDF 1.2) is a draft from December 2025. SSDF doesn't prescribe tools, has four groups (PO, PS, PW, RV) and has not been replaced by any OWASP model.

q: You are introducing controls into 40 repos that have no security checks at all. What is a sensible FIRST control?
options: DAST against all staging environments
Kyverno admission policies for signed images
SLSA L3 provenance for all builds
Secret detection (gitleaks) in the pipeline and a pre-commit hook
explain: Secret detection is cheap, fast and needs little tuning, while the damage from a leaked secret is large. DAST, signatures with admission control and SLSA L3 require much more infrastructure and come later.

q: In a threat modeling session for kurs-shop someone lists: "debug=True in Flask reveals the stack trace and configuration to an attacker." Which STRIDE category is this?
options: Information disclosure
Tampering
Repudiation
Spoofing
explain: Revealing the stack trace and configuration violates confidentiality, so it is Information disclosure. (The Werkzeug debugger can also give code execution, which would be Elevation of privilege, but the problem described is information leakage.)

q: An attacker with write access to a feature branch modifies a Makefile that the test job calls, so the job sends environment variables to their server. Which STRIDE category and which trust boundary are violated?
options: Denial of service; the boundary between the runner and the registry
Repudiation; the boundary between GitLab and Kubernetes
Tampering with code the pipeline executes, resulting in Information disclosure; the boundary between the repo and the runner that holds secrets
Spoofing; the boundary between the developer's laptop and GitLab
explain: Modifying a file the pipeline executes is tampering, and stealing the variables is information disclosure. The critical boundary is between the repo contents (which a less trusted person can change) and the runner that holds secrets. This is indirect Poisoned Pipeline Execution.

q: Match the problem in the kurs-shop repo with the control that first detects it in the pipeline.
options: An f-string in a SQL query in app.py
requests 2.25.1 in requirements.txt
An SG with port 22 open to 0.0.0.0/0 in infra/main.tf
An AWS key in an old commit of config/settings.py
explain: A vulnerable pattern in code is caught by SAST, an old dependency version by SCA, a Terraform misconfiguration by the IaC scanner, and a secret in history by a secret scanner that reads git history. DAST is a distractor: it is late and sees neither Terraform nor git history.

q: Order the controls by the stage in which they naturally run, from earliest to latest.
options: Kyverno verifyImages in the cluster
gitleaks in a pre-commit hook
Trivy image on the built image
ZAP baseline against the staging environment
Semgrep in the merge request pipeline
explain: Pre-commit (secrets) → MR (SAST) → build (image scanning) → staging (DAST) → deploy (admission signature check). Each control sits in the earliest stage where it has something to check.

q: A team asks where to put DAST so it is "as far left as possible." What is the earliest sensible place?
options: In a pre-commit hook, over the source code
After deploy to a short-lived review or staging environment, in the same pipeline
In the MR pipeline before the build job, over the Dockerfile
Only once a year as part of a pentest
explain: DAST needs a running application, so the earliest place is after deploy to a review/staging environment. Pre-commit and the MR before the build have no running application, and a yearly pentest is not a pipeline control.

q: You want SAST, SCA and the IaC scan in the MR to start immediately, in parallel with the build, instead of waiting for the previous stage to finish. What do you add to those jobs?
options: when: always
allow_failure: true
dependencies: []
needs: []
explain: needs: [] means the job has no dependencies and starts as soon as the pipeline starts, regardless of stage. when: always affects whether the job runs after a failure, allow_failure whether a failure blocks, and dependencies: [] only disables downloading artifacts.

q: An IaC gate script returns 0 (clean), 2 (only MEDIUM findings) and 1 (HIGH/CRITICAL). You want MEDIUM to be a yellow warning and HIGH to block. What do you write in the job?
options: allow_failure: true

allow_failure:
  exit_codes: [2]

rules:
  - when: on_failure

allow_failure:
  exit_codes: [1]
explain: allow_failure:exit_codes: [2] allows failure only for exit code 2, so MEDIUM yields a warning and code 1 blocks. allow_failure: true would never block, exit_codes: [1] would let HIGH through, and when: on_failure concerns whether the job runs, not its result.

q: You are running the existing kurs-shop pipeline locally in the lab and first want to see which jobs exist and in which stages. Which command?
options: gitlab-ci-local --list
gitlab-runner list
gitlab-ci-local test
glab ci view
explain: gitlab-ci-local --list prints jobs with their stage and when condition without running them. gitlab-ci-local test would run the test job, gitlab-runner list shows registered runners, and glab ci view works against a real GitLab server, which doesn't exist in the lab.

q: Order the threat modeling steps according to the "four questions" approach.
options: Verify the controls were implemented and repeat when the architecture changes
Draw a data flow diagram with trust boundaries
Decide on controls or risk acceptance
Walk through STRIDE for each trust boundary
explain: What are we working on (diagram) → what can go wrong (STRIDE) → what are we going to do (controls) → did we do a good job (verification and iteration).
